{"id":"PKIX-j72x","title":"pkix-aia-http: async fetcher family (Option C), per the pkix-revocation-http precedent","description":"## Why

pkix-aia-http is synchronous only (ureq). Its sibling pkix-revocation-http shipped a full async trait family in May 2026 under PKIX-a1yc.10. Both crates sit at the same architectural position — a std network adapter implementing a seam whose trait lives in a no_std core crate — so the asymmetry is unjustified.

AIA fetching is latency-bound and chain reassembly (PKIX-zkjb.7) can issue several fetches per validation, so an async consumer (tokio/axum/tower stack) currently has to either block a runtime thread or run AIA reassembly off-thread by hand.

## The existing deferral is filed on a disavowed frame

pkix-aia-http/src/lib.rs:117-119 says:

    //! - **Synchronous only.** An async parallel (mirroring
    //!   `pkix-revocation-http`'s `AsyncHttpCrlFetcher` /
    //!   `AsyncHttpOcspFetcher`) is filed as PKIX-zkjb.5.1, deferred
    //!   until consumer demand surfaces.

'Deferred until consumer demand surfaces' is one of the frames AGENTS.md's 'Project phase and decision framing' section rejects by name: 'No concrete consumer is asking' and 'Wait for consumer demand to drive the API'. That section was added 2026-05-12 after a sweep found closed decisions leaning on post-launch reasoning; this deferral appears to predate or have been missed by that sweep.

Per the prelaunch frame, the async family completes a structural pattern across the two network adapter crates — design closure, not surface bloat. See non-negotiable #6 (callbacks not closed structs) and the AGENTS.md note that YAGNI applies to features, not architecture.

## Shape — copy Option C verbatim

pkix-revocation-http/src/async_fetcher.rs:14-31 records the three options considered and why C won. Apply the same:

- Async traits live in pkix-aia-http (std), NOT in pkix-aia (no_std core). Option A was rejected for propagating async-trait / Send bounds into no_std consumers.
- No block_on bridge. Option B was rejected: 'Calling block_on from inside a running async runtime is a well-known footgun (deadlocks the executor).'
- `AsyncAiaFetcher` as the async analogue of `pkix_aia::AiaFetcher`, gated behind an `async` feature; reference backend behind a separate `client-reqwest-async`-style feature so consumers on hyper/isahc do not pay for reqwest.
- Mirror `batch_fetch`: the sync trait's default-impl is a sequential loop over `fetch` with a documented invitation to override for pipelining (pkix-aia/src/lib.rs:627-646). The async analogue is where that pipelining actually becomes natural — `batch_fetch` should concurrently join rather than loop.

Use `async-trait`, matching pkix-revocation-http; the native-AFIT switch is workspace-wide under PKIX-5hoi, not per-crate.

## Carry over the known defects, do not re-introduce them

Open P1 review findings against the pkix-revocation-http async family — do not copy these:
- PKIX-cr8.1 / PKIX-f1j4.10 — sync CPU work (signature verification) called inside an async fn, blocking the executor for ms-scale CPU
- PKIX-cr8.3 / PKIX-f1j4.5 — async checker default `check_revocation_against_anchor = Ok(())` footgun
- PKIX-f1j4.14 — failures Vec allocated even when the first URL succeeds

## Depends on

Nothing blocking. pkix-aia's AiaFetcher / AiaError surface is stable at 0.1.1.

## Acceptance

[ ] AsyncAiaFetcher behind `async` feature, in pkix-aia-http
[ ] pkix-aia (no_std core) gains no async machinery
[ ] Reference async backend behind its own client feature flag
[ ] async batch_fetch joins concurrently rather than looping
[ ] Destination policy + timeout parity with the sync HttpFetcher (loopback/private/link-local refusal, no redirect following) — see the AiaFetcher Security doc at pkix-aia/src/lib.rs:597-604
[ ] lib.rs:117-119 Limitations text updated; PKIX-zkjb.5.1 reference removed (see PKIX-p2ba)

CLOSED 2026-11-24. pkix-aia-http released at 0.3.0 with the async fetcher family. 41 tests; fmt / clippy --all-targets --all-features / rustdoc -D warnings / typos clean; all three feature combos green.

## Shipped

- `async` feature: AsyncAiaFetcher (the async analogue of pkix_aia::AiaFetcher), NoAsyncAiaFetcher, SyncAsAsync, impl for Arc<T>.
- `client-reqwest-async` feature: AsyncHttpFetcher + GuardedAsyncResolver.
- batch_fetch joins CONCURRENTLY by default, where the sync trait's default loops.
- Both features off by default, so a synchronous consumer pays for neither.
- Option C placement honoured: the async traits live in pkix-aia-http, and pkix-aia gained no async machinery.

## SECURITY FINDING, found and fixed before release

The first implementation had an SSRF hole. GuardedAsyncResolver filters non-public addresses at DNS resolution, mirroring the sync GuardedResolver, and that placement is correct because a resolver-level filter leaves no DNS-rebinding window.

But reqwest DOES NOT consult a custom DNS resolver when the URI host is an IP LITERAL -- there is nothing to resolve, so the connector is reached directly. Result: http://127.0.0.1/, http://10.0.0.1/ and http://169.254.169.254/ bypassed the policy entirely, while http://localhost/ was correctly refused. The default fetcher would have fetched cloud instance metadata on behalf of any peer able to present a certificate.

Found by tests/async_ssrf.rs, written as a case-for-case mirror of tests/review_ssrf.rs precisely because a second implementation of a security policy is where the policy diverges. Three of its ten tests failed on the first run. Had the async family shipped with only a documented claim of parity, this would have shipped with it.

Fix: fetch() checks a literal host before issuing the request. Sound where a pre-request check on a NAME would not be, since a literal cannot change between check and connect; names still go through the resolver. The enforcement flag is derived from the resolver choice rather than stored independently, so the two halves of the policy cannot drift.

Worth generalising: pkix-revocation-http's async family should be checked for the same hole. Its AsyncRevocationFetcher is caller-supplied so it may not apply, but if the reqwest reference backend there applies any destination policy, verify it covers literals. Filed separately.

## Known defects deliberately NOT reproduced

- PKIX-cr8.1 / PKIX-f1j4.10 (sync work inside an async fn blocking the executor): GuardedAsyncResolver uses tokio::net::lookup_host rather than std's blocking ToSocketAddrs, and SyncAsAsync documents explicitly that wrapping HttpFetcher in it is wrong.
- PKIX-cr8.3 / PKIX-f1j4.5 (a default trait method returning Ok(()) and silently skipping a check): AsyncAiaFetcher has one required method and no defaulted security check.
- PKIX-f1j4.14 (failures Vec allocated even when the first URL succeeds): not applicable; batch_fetch returns per-URI results by construction.

## Acceptance

[x] AsyncAiaFetcher behind the `async` feature, in pkix-aia-http
[x] pkix-aia gained no async machinery
[x] Reference async backend behind its own client feature flag
[x] async batch_fetch joins concurrently rather than looping -- asserted by timing three deliberately slow servers, not merely by inspection
[x] Destination policy + timeout parity with the sync HttpFetcher. Verified by a case-for-case mirror of the sync SSRF suite, which is what caught the literal-IP gap. Also covers redirects-not-followed, the response cap at and just over the boundary, and non-HTTP schemes refused before I/O.
[x] lib.rs Limitations text updated; the PKIX-zkjb.5.1 reference removed from lib.rs, Cargo.toml AND README.md -- which closes PKIX-l5ti
[x] All feature combos green, clippy clean, rustdoc clean, typos clean
